catalog_quote: In this section, I describe Abui stress. Phonetically, the stress is characterized by rise in intensity, pitch, and by lengthening. In Abui the stress is assigned in an iambic pattern. In other words, a foot is right-headed and counts at least two morae. The head’s sibling in a right-headed foot counts precisely one mora. The foot system is ‘quantity-sensitive’ which means that any heavy syllable (a syllable with a complex nucleus) projects a foot. Heavy syllables may occur in both word-final and word-medial position. When a foot is projected from a word-medial heavy syllable, the final syllable of the prosodic word is extrametrical. [p. 50] ... Note that a closed syllable in the word kokda ‘younger sibling’ above does not influence the foot pattern. Recall that only bimoraic nuclei project the head of a foot. [p. 52] ... In sum, the Abui metric pattern is iambic. The stress is primarily realized with lengthenin[g], secondarily with raised pitch and finally with increased intensity. Bimoraic syllables attract stress because of their length, which is the only significant characteristic of the stressed syllable. [p. 58] ... Abui prosodic words are stressed following the iambic pattern, with an optional extrametrical syllable. Bimoraic nuclei are heavy and attract stress. [p. 64] ... The extrametricality is triggered by a heavy syllable in penultimate position. As the majority of words have a light syllable in this position, extrametricality is rare. [p. 65]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (563 pp., text, the PDF's metadata gives the title 'A grammar of Abui v.7.0'). extracted text of PDF page 72 = printed p. 50 shows the heading '2.5 Stress' followed word for word by the quoted paragraph ('In this section, I describe Abui stress. Phonetically, the stress is characterized by rise in intensity, pitch, and by lengthening. In Abui the stress is assigned in an iambic pattern.. When a foot is projected from a word-medial heavy syllable, the final syllable of the prosodic word is extrametrical.'). I read the whole of 2.5 (pp. 50-65, PDF 72-87): 2.5.1 light monosyllables unstressed in isolation, heavy monosyllables project a foot (ya, lung vs bui, yaa); 2.5.2 iambic feet, final…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive iambic stress built right-to-left over the prosodic word. Heavy syllables are those with a bimoraic (long-vowel or vowel-sequence) nucleus; closed CVC syllables count as light. In words made only of light syllables the final syllable is stressed (anu 'market' [ʔɑ'nu], kokda [kɔk'dɑ], mahiting 'meat' [mɑhɪ'tɪŋ], malatai [mɑlɑ'tɑɪ]); a heavy syllable attracts stress wherever it stands, so a heavy penult is stressed and the final light syllable is extrametrical (feela 'friend' ['feːlɑ], naana 'older sibling', talaama 'six' [tɑ'laːmɑ]). Conclusion p. 64: 'Abui prosodic words are stressed following the iambic pattern, with an optional extrametrical syllable. Bimoraic nuclei are heavy and attract stress.' Stress is realized primarily by length, then raised pitch, then intensity (p. 58, instrumental Figures 4-13).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; trisyllabic words are parsed into two feet in the bracketed grids of (103), p. 64 (e.g. (l)(l *l)), but no secondary stress is marked or mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: Light monosyllables (ya 'water', lung 'door') do not attract stress in isolation but can be stressed as the last member of a prosodic unit (2.5.1, pp. 50-51); heavy monosyllables project a foot. Affixes and clitics are light and do not attract stress, but aspectual clitics form one prosodic word with the verb and take the final stress (tukon [tu'kɔn] vs tukon-i [tukɔ'nɪ], marang=te [mɑrɑŋ'tɛ]) (2.5.6, pp. 62-63). A small number of mono- and disyllabic words carry lexical tone in addition (2.5.4, pp. 58-62: ía 'moon' vs ì-a 'put down'). Under stress /ɛ/ breaks to [ɛɑ] in fast speech (2.5.5). Extrametrical heavy syllables 'also tend to have high pitch' (p. 58).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word (stem plus pronominal prefixes and aspect clitics); words recorded in citation and in a fixed syntactic frame; instrumental figures from single tokens of adult speakers. Describes the Takalelang dialect (Kratochvíl 2007:24).
new_statements.identity_note: Kratochvíl 2007 explicitly describes the Takalelang dialect of Abui (p. 24: 'present work describes the Takalelang dialect'); the language-level glottocode is abui1241 (no separate Glottolog code for Takalelang seen). Stokhof 1984 covers the Ateng Melang dialect, which Kratochvíl notes differs in phoneme inventory.

tone_statements.quote: The paper shows that there are at least found different tone contours (Low, Mid, High, and Falling) whose distribution is not fixed lexically but alternates with inflection and syntactic environment. [...] The distribution of pitch contours is not predictable from the segmental make-up of a root, and the pitch therefore has to be considered lexicalized. On the other hand, certain regularities exist in sensitivity of the peak alignment to the length of preceding syllables and minimal pairs are relatively sparse. We will argue that Abui is a low-density lexical tone language, which means that tone is lexicalized only with certain syllables, although we have not developed an abstract model yet.

tone_statements.quote: The third chapter examines lexical tone in Abui. Abui is a low-density lexical tone language, which means that tone is associated only with certain syllables and minimal pairs are relatively sparse. The chapter surveys known tone systems and characterizes the Abui type. Further, the chapter examines how lexical tone is affected by derivational (compounding) and inflectional processes (person and aspect inflection). The fourth chapter examines the behavior of lexical tones in the context of the sentence, where a number of phrasal tones are identified, not unlike in the recently described and related Fataluku language of East Timor.

tone_statements.quote: The phonetic characteristics of stress involve intensity, pitch, and lengthening. Stress assignment is based on an iambic pattern (Kratochvíl, 2007). Stress is assigned to the final syllable when a word consists of a two light syllables, as in (24), or a light syllable followed by a heavy syllable, as in (25) (from Kratochvíl, 2007, pp. 51-52). [...] In disyllabic and trisyllabic prosodic words containing a heavy syllable followed by a light syllable, stress is assigned to the penultimate, heavy syllable, as in (27a) (from Kratochvíl, 2007, pp. 55-56). [...] Examples (28a-b) show a minimal pair illustrating how stress assignment is closely linked to vowel length. Example (28a) shows the iambic pattern of final stress, while (28b) shows how the heavy syllable containing a long vowel attracts stress. (28) a. /fa.ˈlɪŋ/ faling 'axe' b. /ˈfaː.lɪŋ/ faaling 'listen to'

sources.quote: The base form sama 'same' has also been borrowed into Abui and is used by older speakers. It appears to be fully integrated into Abui and it differs suprasegmentally from Malay sama 'same'. In the Abui sama [sa'ma:], the second syllable is prominent, while in Malay ['sa:ma], the first syllable is prominent (thanks to Frantisek Kratochvil for pointing this out). || Note also that Abui has a quinary (base-5) system, where the numerals 'seven', 'eight', and 'nine' are compounds containing a form for 'five' in their first position followed by a form reflecting 'two', 'three', and 'four'. In distributive reduplication, only this second element, which carries word stress, is reduplicated, resulting in a type of internal reduplication.

sources.note: Revises Kratochvil 2007's tone statements from Delpada 2016: at least four tone contours (Low, Mid, High, Falling) whose distribution alternates with inflection (person, aspect), derivation (inchoative, compounding) and syntax (focus, phrase boundaries); pitch is not predictable from segments hence lexicalised, but minimal pairs are sparse - Abui is a 'low-density lexical tone language'; example paradigm of afu 'fish' across nine environments; parallels with Fataluku; keywords include grammatical tone and tonogenesis.

sources.note: The thesis is about lexical and grammatical tone in Abui; ch. 3 argues Abui is a low-density lexical tone language (tone associated only with certain syllables, sparse minimal pairs) and examines how lexical tone is affected by compounding and person/aspect inflection; ch. 4 identifies phrasal (boundary) tones interacting with lexical tone and syntax, compared with Fataluku. Saad 2020:168 (held) reproduces its minimal pairs ia 'moon' (H) vs i-a 'put' (L), lak 'break' (H) vs lak 'mark' (L), fir 'star' vs fir 'rush' (Delpada 2016:69) and the possessive-prefix H-shift (p. 76).
